correctness.rationale: The quadratic-order Frobenius congruence \(Q_{\ell m}\equiv Q_m\pmod\ell\) holds for every odd prime \(\ell\). The trace binomial expansion proves exact lifting \(\nu_\ell(Q_{\ell m})=\nu_\ell(Q_m)+1\) when \(\ell\mid Q_m\). For the smaller odd prime \(p<q\), the finite-field quotient \((1+\sqrt2)/(1-\sqrt2)\) has multiplicative order dividing \(p-1\) or \(p+1<q\); a \(q\)-power cannot raise it to \(-1\) unless \(\alpha+\beta=0\), impossible for odd \(p\). This excludes \(p\) and proves the \(q^b\)-or-\(1\) dichotomy. The prime-power and \(p=2\) cases use Frobenius and parity; the infinite counterexample family follows symbolically from the doubling identity. Finite modular checks test the theorem through \(30000\) and for seven much larger indices but do not replace the unrestricted proof.

originality.rationale: Section 6.2 of arXiv:2301.05758v1 explicitly asks for index-gcd closed forms and conjectures a rank criterion. The theorem supplies an exact classification on every one- or two-prime-support index and rigorously refutes the suggested sufficient condition on an infinite family. Inspected relevant primary PDF sections, Lucas period work, polynomial strong divisibility literature, published mathematical-record searches and related scholarly claims; no implication-equivalent universal formula was found. Residual risk remains from classical implicit Lucas companion arithmetic outside indexed sources.
residual_risks: An equivalent two-prime-support classification could occur as an unindexed older Lucas companion corollary.
The source conjecture might have an independent correction published elsewhere not surfaced by targeted searches.

value.rationale: This exact classification of every index having at most two distinct prime divisors resolves a natural infinite domain of Mbirika--Schrader--Spilker Question 31. The all-or-none prime-power rule strengthens a divisibility-only criterion and provides an effective test from \(Q_{p^a}\pmod q\) rather than computing the full term. The infinite \(3\cdot2^a\) family for \(a\ge2\) refutes a published rank criterion, so the motivation is substantive rather than a small arbitrary numerical gain.
